original_summary: Nyet! is a trick-taking card game for 2 to 5 players. Each round, players take turns placing veto tokens to fix the round's rules: first player, discard rule, trump, supertrump and points per trick. The first player then forms uneven teams, and the teams score tricks and captured 1s ('Loot') over 8 to 10 rounds.

review.evidence: Original: the veto phase and team choice give real decisions, and no single veto policy wins. However, the first player both picks the teams and hands out the doubling Bonus card, which is a strong seat edge each round. The previous 3-player variation was worse: in Nyet the Pair's 2 names against the Lone's 1 let the Pair alone fix supertrump and push trump onto the Lone's short colour. 'Pair names the Lone's long colours' was then close to a dominant policy, and the Lone's choices barely mattered.

Original: card play rewards skill, but full random deals of 60 cards plus team composition make single rounds very noisy. Previous variation: the testers estimated 60-70% of the result came from each player's single blind Lone deal. An informed Pair held the Lone to about 0-0.5 tricks, against 1-2 for a blind Pair. So the winner was whoever got the best blind hand.
Trick play has deep headroom: counting cards, reading voids, timing the supertrump 1, choosing when to lead trump. A weak player still wins some tricks with good cards.

Hands are hidden. Players infer voids from what is followed, and the veto phase reveals preferences. Previous variation: there was something to infer, but information was unequal between seats, so inference could not overcome the leak.
Trick winners and scores follow arithmetically from colour and number. No judge is needed.

Original: a 5-line veto board, team selection, Bonus cards, discard/pass rules and 60 cards with 8-10 long rounds exceed the step limits. Previous variation: it fit the limits (36 one-trick rounds, 24 cards) but needed fixes for fairness.

problems: P1 Information leak: in the 2nd and 3rd deals of a set, Pair members already know the Lone Hand L card for card. The three plays of L therefore happen under different information, so the duplicate comparison is unfair.
P2 Nyet shut the Lone out: with 2 names against 1, the Pair fixed supertrump and blocked the Lone's best trump colours. The Lone's one decision outside card play was meaningless.
P3 Deal luck in the Pair hands: the 19 non-L cards were reshuffled each deal with 9 set aside unseen, so trump length against the same L varied widely between the three plays.

P4 Any fix that fixes the set-aside cards but keeps them hidden creates a new leak: after deal 1, players have seen most of the Pair's cards. So the later Lones would know the Pair's card pool and the first Lone would not.
P5 The PairTricks tie-break was largely decided by the draw (random splits), so ties were settled by luck.
P6 Simultaneous talk added little: Pair members were already informed, and talk let them share the leaked L.

changes.what: The Lone's 5 cards are face up to all players in every deal, including the first of each set.
changes.why: All three plays of L now happen with everyone knowing L, so they are identical in information.

changes.what: At the start of each set, the deck is shuffled once into L (5 cards), a Reserve of 9 cards that stays out all set, and a Pair Pool of 10 cards. The Reserve is shown face up to everyone. Each deal of the set, only the Pair Pool is reshuffled and split 5/5 between the two Pair members.
changes.why: Every Lone faces the same 10 opposing cards, so trump length against L is identical across the set. Making the Reserve public tells every Lone, including the first, exactly which cards oppose them. Deal 1 therefore leaks nothing that later Lones lack. Only the 5/5 split is hidden from the Lone.
changes.fixes: P3 Deal luck in the Pair hands; P4

changes.what: New Nyet. The two Pair members secretly and at the same moment each name one colour, and the names are revealed. Supertrump is the colour they named; if they named different colours, it is the one earlier in the set's priority order. Both named colours are barred. The Lone then chooses trump from the unnamed colours, of which there are always 2 or 3.
changes.why: The Pair still vetoes, which keeps the Nyet idea. The Lone now has real control: they weigh L against the known Pair Pool and against what the Pair's names suggest about the hidden split.
changes.fixes: P2 Nyet shut the Lone out

changes.what: The winner is decided by total LoneTricks alone. Equal highest totals are a draw. PairTricks is still recorded but does not decide anything.
changes.why: Each player is Lone exactly once per set with the same L, so comparing LoneTricks is already a duplicate comparison. Subtracting a set average would change nothing, because the same average is subtracted from everyone. Removing the tie-break removes the luck it carried.

Each Pair member knows their own 5 cards, L and the Reserve, so they can work out their partner's hand. They have nothing to coordinate by talk. Anything they say is seen by the Lone and serves only to mislead, so a rational Lone ignores it. Talk fails the reasoning test. The Pair's Nyet names already serve as costly, informative signals.

keeps: The Nyet idea: players veto colours, and what is left becomes the round's trump and supertrump.
Trump plus a supertrump whose 1 beats every trump.
Following the led colour, and highest trump, otherwise highest of the led colour, wins.
The uneven 1-against-2 team structure (the small team against the larger team) that rotates every deal.
Duplicate structure: each player plays the same Lone hand once per set, so the hand's quality cancels out.

recommendation.reason: The previous version's failure came from unequal information and a lopsided Nyet. Both can be fixed inside the limits by making L and the Reserve public, fixing the Pair Pool for each set, and giving the Lone the trump choice.

variation.name: Nyet! Duplicate Lone (Open Reserve)
variation.summary: Three players take turns as the Lone against a Pair in 4-trick deals. Within each set of three deals, every player plays the same Lone hand against the same 10 opposing cards. The Pair vetoes colours and sets the supertrump, the Lone picks trump, and the player with the most tricks won as Lone wins.
variation.rules:
PLAYERS AND CARDS: There are 3 players in seats 1, 2 and 3, sitting clockwise. The deck has 24 unique cards in four colours (Red, Yellow, Green, Blue), each colour numbered 1 to 6. Each player has two counters, LoneTricks and PairTricks, both starting at 0.

STRUCTURE: There are 9 deals of 4 tricks each, 36 rounds in all, and each round is one trick. The deals form 3 sets: set 1 is deals 1-3, set 2 is deals 4-6 and set 3 is deals 7-9.

LONE ORDER: The Lone for deals 1 to 9 is seat 1, 2, 3, 2, 3, 1, 3, 1, 2. The other two players form the Pair. The Pair member to the Lone's left (clockwise) is Pair-Left; the other is Pair-Right.

COLOUR PRIORITY: Set 1 uses Red, Yellow, Green, Blue. Set 2 uses Yellow, Green, Blue, Red. Set 3 uses Green, Blue, Red, Yellow.

START OF A DEAL (before the first trick of each deal only):
(a) DEAL. In the first deal of a set: shuffle all 24 cards. The first 5 become this set's Lone Hand L. The next 9 become this set's Reserve. The last 10 become this set's Pair Pool, dealt 5 to Pair-Left and 5 to Pair-Right. In the second and third deals of a set: the Lone receives exactly the cards of L, the Reserve is unchanged, and only the 10 Pair Pool cards are shuffled and dealt 5 to Pair-Left and 5 to Pair-Right.
(b) OPEN CARDS. The Lone's 5 cards and the 9 Reserve cards are shown face up to all players for the whole deal. Reserve cards are never played. Each Pair member's hand is seen only by that Pair member. Everyone therefore knows which 10 cards the Pair holds together, but only the Pair knows how they are split.
(c) NYET. Pair-Left and Pair-Right at the same moment each secretly name one colour. Both names are then revealed.
(d) SUPERTRUMP. If both named the same colour, that colour is supertrump. If they named different colours, supertrump is the named colour that comes first in the set's priority order. Every named colour is barred from being trump.
(e) TRUMP. The Lone chooses trump from the colours nobody named, of which there are 3 or 2. Trump and supertrump are therefore always different colours.
(f) Trump and supertrump are announced. Pair-Left leads the first trick.

EACH TRICK:
(1) The leader plays any one card from hand face up. Its colour is the led colour.
(2) The other two players then each choose one card at the same moment, seeing the led card but not each other's choice. Both cards are then revealed.
(3) FOLLOWING: a player holding a card of the led colour must play one. Otherwise they may play any card.

WINNING A TRICK:
- If the 1 of the supertrump colour was played, it wins. Other supertrump cards are ordinary cards of their colour.
- Otherwise, if any trump was played, the highest-numbered trump wins.
- Otherwise, the highest-numbered card of the led colour wins.
- Ties cannot occur, because every card is unique.
- The winner leads the next trick of the same deal.

SCORING EACH TRICK: If the Lone wins the trick, the Lone's LoneTricks rises by 1. If a Pair member wins it, that member's PairTricks rises by 1.

ANNOUNCEMENT: After each trick, all three cards, the winner and every player's counters are shown to everyone.

END OF DEAL: After the 4th trick, each player's remaining card is discarded unseen. Reserve cards stay out until the set ends.

END OF GAME: The game ends after trick 36.
variation.objective: The player with the highest LoneTricks total wins. If two or three players share the highest LoneTricks, the game is a draw among them. PairTricks does not affect the result.
variation.expected_effect: Each player is Lone exactly once per set, holding the same L against the same 10 Pair cards, with the same public knowledge. Seats differ only by the hidden 5/5 split and by skill, so hand quality cancels out. The Pair still vetoes: they name colours to grab a supertrump 1 they hold, or to block the Lone's long colour. Every veto spends their choice of supertrump. The Lone reads the split from the names: a Pair naming Green may hold the Green 1, or may be protecting a Green void. The Lone then picks trump against the known pool, and in play reads voids, counts the 10 known cards and judges when the supertrump 1 is still out. Simple policies lose. A Lone who always picks the first allowed trump falls behind one who matches trump to L. A Pair that always names the first priority colour leaves the Lone a free choice of 3. A player who always plays their highest card wastes trumps. The play order rotates by set, so each seat is first, second and third Lone once and no seat gains from watching others play L first. Talk is omitted because the Pair is fully informed and talk could only be cheap bluffing that the Lone would rightly ignore.

balanced.evidence:
SCORE IDENTITY. Let L_X be the total tricks player X wins as Lone over X's two Lone deals (0 to 8). In a deal where another player is Lone, each pair member scores 4 minus that Lone's tricks. So A = 2*L_A + (8 - L_B) + (8 - L_C) = 16 + 2*L_A - L_B - L_C, and A - B = 3*(L_A - L_B). The winner is simply the player with the most tricks won as Lone. The 2-versus-1+1 labelling is consistent with this.

PAIR INCENTIVE. Every trick denied to the Lone gives both pair members +1 and costs the Lone 2, so the pair always wants to minimise L. Helping your partner does not hurt you, because you score exactly what your partner scores in that deal. No late-round betrayal problem arises: the roles are fixed per deal.

SEAT AND ORDER. The Lone order 1,2,3,3,2,1 makes each seat Lone exactly twice. The pair always has the opening lead of each deal. Because the roles rotate evenly, no seat has a structural edge. The priority rotation is independent of the random deal.

THOUGHTLESS POLICIES, by the winner rule:
(i) Always Nyet the first priority colour. This only pushes trump to the second colour. It does not stop an opponent who holds the supertrump 1 or long trumps from out-tricking you as Lone, so it can lose.
(ii) Always play the highest legal card. As Lone, this wastes high cards into tricks the pair will trump. As a pair member, it overtakes a partner who is already winning. A careful Lone who holds back the supertrump 1 or a trump beats it. It loses some games and wins some.
(iii) Always play the lowest card. This concedes tricks whenever you lead as Lone, so L stays near 0 and it loses to almost anything.
No Nyet colour and no card rule wins or draws whatever the opponents do. Each colour's value depends on your hand and on the others' votes.

CAVEAT. Each L_X is a small integer, mostly 0 to 4, so ties for the top are frequent. This is a luck issue, treated below. Every player can realistically win. Pass.

playable.evidence:
WHAT WORKS.
- Limits are met: 12 steps, 4 choice steps (one Nyet poll plus three card plays), 15 attributes, 1 hidden element (hands), 1 random draw (the shuffle at deal start, gated by a `when` on trick 1 of each deal), 24 rounds (40 allowed).
- Dealing uses the shared_deck_draw workaround. The supertrump vote count with a priority tie-break and the trick-winner logic need calc steps; 12 is tight but plausible. Following suit can be a referee check, but the trick winner and the scores must be computed arithmetically, and the design should state that.
- The rules are complete for every case. All three name one colour: that colour is supertrump, and trump is the first unnamed colour. Three different colours: a three-way tie, broken by priority. Only the supertrump 1 is special; other supertrump-colour cards are ordinary.
- The game is finite, with no board and no clock.

THE FAILURE: no talk where it is needed. With three players the design opens no round with talk. Yet the Nyet vote is exactly a disagreement point:
- The Lone and the pair want different trump and supertrump colours.
- The two pair members need to coordinate. With two votes on the same colour they control supertrump, and their naming jointly controls which colour becomes trump.
- They cannot see each other's hands and cannot communicate, so a pair member can only guess the partner's Nyet. A split pair vote (three different colours) hands the result to the priority tie-break.
Talk would give real material to reason about: claims about your hand, possible bluffing by the Lone, and a cost to following a proposal that does not fit your hand. This is the case where talk is missing and players can only guess each other.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
THE WINNER DEPENDS ON TWO RANDOM HANDS. The winner is the player with the most Lone tricks, and each player gets only two Lone deals of four cards. Half the deck (12 cards) is set aside unseen, so trump length varies widely from deal to deal.

DECISIONS ARE SHALLOW.
- Holding the supertrump 1 is a near-guaranteed trick. A Lone with no trump or one trump, and no supertrump 1, usually takes 0 tricks against 8 pair cards when the pair has the opening lead.
- With four cards and forced following, most card play is nearly forced. The real decisions are one Nyet vote per deal and perhaps one or two discretionary plays.

ROUGH ESTIMATE.
- A Lone's trick count from hand quality spans about 0 to 3 per deal, so roughly 0 to 6 over two deals.
- A skilled Lone might gain perhaps 0.3 to 0.5 tricks per deal over a naive one, so about 1 trick in total.
- Most of the outcome is therefore the deal: perhaps 60 to 70% chance.

UNDER EQUAL GOOD PLAY. If all three play well, each L_X is set by the strength of the two Lone hands that player was dealt. The winner is then decided by the deal alone, and ties for the top (frequent, about a quarter to a third of games) end in draws. The design does not equalise hands across players. A good player is not clearly favoured.

WHAT CAN BE INFERRED. Something exists: the others' Nyet votes reveal their holdings, and played cards narrow down the 12 unseen cards. But this is too thin and comes too late to outweigh the hand variance, because the votes are revealed only after trump is fixed.

required_changes: Reasoning_over_luck: make the Lone hands duplicate. At each shuffle, store the three 4-card hands in a game list. Replay the same deal, with the same set-aside cards, three times, rotating so that each player plays the identical Lone hand once against the same two pair hands. For example, deals 1-3 use deal A with Lone 1, 2, 3, and deals 4-6 use deal B with Lone 3, 2, 1. This keeps 6 deals and 24 tricks. Deciding the winner by the most Lone tricks then compares players on identical cards.

Reasoning_over_luck: deepen each deal so that card play matters more. Either deal 6 cards to each player (18 dealt, 6 set aside) and play 5 tricks per deal after each player discards 1, or play 6 tricks per deal with fewer deals. Stay within 40 rounds, for example 6 deals x 6 tricks = 36.

Reasoning_over_luck: replace the plain draw with a reasoning-based tie-break. For example, a tie on Lone tricks goes to whoever conceded fewer tricks to the Lone while in the pair. Draws should then be rare.

Playable: add one simultaneous talk step at the start of each deal, before the Nyet poll. Either all three write at the same time and all messages are shown, or each pair member gets a private_channel message to the partner. Pair members can then coordinate their Nyet votes, and the Lone can bluff, instead of everyone guessing. State that talk is not binding.

Playable: state explicitly that calc steps compute the trick winner and all scores arithmetically from card colour and number. Only follow-suit legality may be a referee check. Confirm that the deal, the vote count with the priority tie-break, and the trick resolution fit within 12 steps, and within 20 if duplicate hands are added.

balanced.evidence:
Seat rotation (Lone for deals 1-9 = 1,2,3,2,3,1,3,1,2): every seat is Lone exactly 3 times (12 tricks), once in each position of a set. Seat 1 is 1st, 3rd and 2nd Lone; seat 2 is 2nd, 1st and 3rd; seat 3 is 3rd, 2nd and 1st. Every seat is Pair-Left 3 times and Pair-Right 3 times (deal 1 PL=2, d2 PL=3, d3 PL=1, d4 PL=3, d5 PL=1, d6 PL=2, d7 PL=1, d8 PL=2, d9 PL=3). So no seat has a structural edge over the whole game.
Payoff ordering: score = 25*LoneTricks + PairTricks, and PairTricks <= 24, so LoneTricks dominates as stated. The arithmetic is consistent.
Trump checks: supertrump is a named colour and trump is an unnamed one, so they always differ. With 3 names out of 4 colours, at least 1 colour is unnamed. Cards are unique, so tricks have no ties.
Thoughtless policies under the WINNER RULE:
(a) Always name the first priority colour (Red in set 1). Against a Pair that also blocks the Lone's best colour, the Lone gets the 2nd or 3rd unnamed colour, which is usually not its long suit. The policy loses deals and does not guarantee a win or draw.
(b) Always play the highest legal card. As a Pair follower it often overtakes its own partner, since followers choose simultaneously, and wastes high cards. Against sensible play it loses Lone deals. Against random play it usually wins, which is expected in a trick-taking game but is not a never-loses policy.
(c) Always lead the lowest card. As Lone it gives up the lead and loses.
No option is dominant: following is forced, and the best trick play depends on the voids and trump left. No thoughtless policy wins or draws against every opponent action.
Rough trick table for one 4-trick deal:
- Lone holding 2+ high trumps with a blind Pair: about 2 tricks.
- Lone holding 0-1 trumps: about 0-1 tricks.
All three players can realistically win.
Smaller concern: kingmaking in deal 9. A Pair member with no chance can throw tricks to the Lone. This is not decisive.

playable.evidence:
The rules cover dealing, the duplicate Lone hand, talk, Nyet, the trump and supertrump derivation (with a tie rule), leading, following, trick resolution (supertrump 1 > highest trump > highest led-colour card), the next leader, discards and the end. The game is finite (36 tricks) and decided by arithmetic on the counters the game keeps.
Limits:
- steps_per_round 17 <= 20
- choice_steps_per_round 4 <= 4 (talk, Nyet, lead, simultaneous follow; talk and Nyet use a `when` condition on the first trick of a deal)
- attributes 18 <= 20 (6 counters plus trump, supertrump, led colour, leader, deal index, L, three hands, aside, trick cards; tight but plausible)
- hidden_elements 1 (hidden hands)
- random_draws_per_round 1 (one shuffle at the start of a deal)
- rounds 36 <= 40
The follow-suit rule is enforceable by the engine. No board, clock or judge is needed.
Talk with 3 players is justified: the Lone and the Pair disagree about trump, so following a proposal can cost a player, and bluffing about holdings gives material to reason about. Talk is simultaneous, as required.
The followers' simultaneous choice is stated explicitly. The game is not a cooperation dilemma, so the late-round betrayal test does not apply.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
The duplicate scheme does not cancel luck. It creates an information asymmetry that turns luck into the decider.
In the first deal of a set, the Pair has not seen L. In the second deal, one Pair member (the previous Lone) knows L card for card. In the third deal, both Pair members know L completely, and simultaneous talk lets them share it.
Nyet arithmetic: the Pair has 2 names against the Lone's 1. The Pair alone decides supertrump, since 2 votes beat 1. It can also block two colours, so trump falls to the first priority colour outside the two Pair names and the Lone's name. A Pair that knows L names the Lone's long suit(s), so trump lands on a colour where the Lone is short or void. The Lone with its single name cannot stop this.
Estimates:
- Lone facing an informed Pair: about 0-0.5 tricks per deal.
- Lone facing a blind Pair: about 1-2 tricks per deal, depending on L.
Result under good play: almost all LoneTricks come from each player's single blind deal. That deal's L is a fresh random 5-card hand that is never replayed under the same conditions, since the other two players play it informed. Each seat's blind L comes from a different set. So when all three play well, the winner is mostly whoever was dealt the strongest blind L, which is a random draw.
Further chance: the Pair hands are reshuffled from 19 cards every deal, with 9 cards set aside, so trump length against the Lone varies widely even for the same L. Ties on LoneTricks then fall to PairTricks, which are also largely draw-driven.
Estimate: 60-70% of the result is decided by the deal and the position-hand coupling, not by inference or planning. There is something to infer (the Pair's voids, bluffs in talk), but a Lone who reasons well cannot overcome an informed 2-vote Pair.

required_changes: Remove the information leak: in EVERY deal, including the first of each set, place the Lone's 5 cards face up to all players before talk. All three plays of L then happen under identical information, and the duplicate comparison is fair.

Give the Lone real control in Nyet. For example: each Pair member secretly names one colour, then the Lone chooses trump from the colours the Pair did not name (always at least 2), and supertrump is the colour the Pair named (tie broken by priority). The Lone's reasoning about the Pair's hidden hands then decides trump, instead of the Pair's 2-to-1 vote shutting the Lone out.

To further cut deal luck, keep the 9 set-aside cards fixed for all three deals of a set, and re-deal only the 10 Pair cards between the two Pair members. Alternatively, score each Lone deal relative to the set average (LoneTricks minus the mean of the three Lones' tricks with that L) so that only performance differences count.

balanced.evidence:
WHAT IS DECIDED: Only LoneTricks counts. In any deal the Lone wants tricks and both Pair members want the Lone to take none, because every point the Lone scores is a rival's point. PairTricks is inert.

SEAT EDGE FROM LONE ORDER: Within a set, the same L and the same Reserve are faced by every seat as Lone. Position in each set's Lone order:
| seat | set 1 | set 2 | set 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1st | 3rd | 2nd |
| 2 | 2nd | 1st | 3rd |
| 3 | 3rd | 2nd | 1st |
Each seat is first, second and third once. Every seat is Pair-Left or Pair-Right as often as the others, and every seat is Lone 3 times (9 deals x 4 tricks = 36 tricks, 12 as Lone each). Move order, being led into by Pair-Left, and information asymmetries are therefore identical for all seats. The Lone always being led into is a handicap all three suffer equally.

MAIN DECISION, NYET TABLE (Pair view, Lone's 5 cards open):
| Pair names | colours barred | Lone picks trump from |
|---|---|---|
| same colour X | 1 | 3 colours |
| X and Y | 2 | 2 colours |
Naming two different colours (the Lone's two longest or strongest suits) dominates for the Pair. Which one becomes supertrump is fixed by priority, so the Pair also wants the supertrump 1 in its own hands or in the Reserve. There is no single colour that is always best: it depends on L and on where the six 1s lie. So no fixed 'always name the first colour' policy is optimal, and miscoordinating (both naming the same colour) costs the Pair.

ROUGH LONE EXPECTATION: 5 open cards, trump forced into one of its two weaker colours, facing 10 cards held by two cooperating players with full information. Typically 0-2 tricks per deal, about 1, so about 9 over 9 Lone deals... more precisely, each player plays 9 deals in total but is Lone in 3 per set.

THOUGHTLESS POLICIES UNDER THE WINNER RULE:
- Lone 'always lead/play highest': wastes high cards into higher trumps and the supertrump 1. Against sensible Lones on the same L it scores fewer or equal LoneTricks, so it loses or draws.
- Lone 'always lowest': never wins a contested trick and loses.
- Pair 'always play first legal card': gifts the rival Lone tricks. That raises the rival's total, so it loses or draws against careful Pair play.
- 'Always name Red': often bars a weak Lone colour, letting the Lone trump in its long suit, and loses ground.
No policy never loses, no option is strictly dominant, and every seat can realistically win.

playable.evidence:
CARD COUNT: 5 + 9 + 10 = 24. The Lone plays 4 of 5 cards, as does each Pair member. The leader rule, the follow rule, trick precedence (supertrump 1, then highest trump, then highest led colour), the next leader, Nyet resolution and the trump choice are all defined. Ties are impossible.

START-OF-DEAL AND START-OF-SET STEPS: These can be carried by per-step `when` conditions on the round number. No block switching is needed.

LIMITS:
| limit | design | cap |
|---|---|---|
| steps_per_round | 16 | 20 |
| choice steps | 4 (Nyet poll, trump, lead, simultaneous follow poll) | 4 |
| attributes | 12 | 20 |
| hidden_elements | 1 (the Pair split, hidden only from the Lone, since each Pair member deduces the partner's hand by subtraction) | 3 |
| random draws | 1 shuffle, at most once per round | 1 |
| rounds | 36 | 40 |

The game is finite, scored by arithmetic, and needs no board, judge or clock.

TALK: With 3 players, having no talk is defensible. The Pair are aligned and both see everything, so they can compute the same Nyet. Open talk would only tell the Lone the Pair's plan. Simultaneous follows are correctly polls.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
WHAT THE DUPLICATE FIXES: L and the Reserve are identical for the three Lones in a set, so luck of the Lone hand is cancelled.

WHAT IT DOES NOT FIX: The 10-card Pair Pool is reshuffled between Pair-Left and Pair-Right every deal. Each Lone therefore faces a different split. Who holds the supertrump 1, the trump length, and voids that let the Pair ruff or overtake the Lone all swing the Lone's result by about 0-2 tricks on the same L.

GOOD PLAY BY ALL: If all three play the intended strategy (optimal Nyet, optimal trump, card play), the only difference between their LoneTricks totals is the 9 independent splits.
- Per-set differences are about +/-1 trick.
- Totals are small (about 0-6), so these differences decide the winner or create a draw.
- A modest skill edge (better split inference from the simultaneous follows) is of the same order as the split noise.

CONCLUSION: The winner under equal good play is set by the random deal alone, which fails the check. Chance accounts for roughly half or more of decisive outcomes.

WHAT IS GOOD: The inference content is real. The Lone infers the hidden split from follows and voids, and the Pair coordinates its Nyet blind.

required_changes: Fix the Pair split per set: at the first deal of a set, deal the Pool into hand A (5 cards) and hand B (5 cards). In every deal of that set, give A to Pair-Left and B to Pair-Right, so all three Lones face an identical position.

Because the two players who were Pair in deal 1 then know the split, make A and B visible to all three players at the start of each set. Equal information removes the order advantage. Inference then comes from the simultaneous follows and the Nyet coordination rather than from the deal.

Optionally, to cut the many draws from small totals, add a tie-break in LoneTricks ties: the fewest tricks conceded as Pair, i.e. LoneTricks scored against you while you were in the Pair. This is computed arithmetically.
